title: Corpus Christi
hookLine: Catholics carry the sacrament through the streets in procession

lines: A BELL, AND THE STREET GOES QUIET.
cards: A small bell rings at the corner, and the street goes quiet.

Down the road, over a carpet of petals someone spent all night laying out, comes a procession: children in white, a band, candles, and under a canopy on poles, a priest holding something gold and shining.
In its center is a small round wafer of bread. As it passes, people on the sidewalk kneel. A man on a bike takes off his cap.
This happens in some Catholic towns and parishes on one feast, whose name is just two Latin words. Today, Corpus Christi.

teach.h: CORPUS CHRISTI: THE BODY OF CHRIST.
teach.b: Corpus Christi is Latin for the body of Christ. The words go back to the night before Jesus died.
Paul passes them on, in the King James Bible: Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said, "this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me."
In John, Jesus says, "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." Christians understand those words in more than one way.
Catholic teaching holds that at Mass the bread truly becomes the body of Christ, and that he remains present in it afterward.
So the consecrated host can be kept, honored and carried, and on this feast it goes out through the streets.
Orthodox Christians also speak of the bread truly becoming Christ's body, though this procession belongs to the Western calendar, and some Anglican churches mark the day too.
Other Protestants understand communion as a remembrance, or as Christ present by the Spirit to those who receive it, and wouldn't carry the bread in procession.

Each takes the words seriously; they hear them differently. For those who keep it, the procession says: what happens at the altar isn't meant to stay behind the church doors. It goes past the bakery and the bus stop.
That fits the week: two friends who knew him in the breaking of bread at Emmaus, a parish walking its boundaries, a street crowd hearing the news in their own languages.
Again and again, the holy went outside.

how: On Corpus Christi some Catholic parishes carry the consecrated host in a monstrance through the streets under a canopy, with hymns, candles and stops for prayer along the way.

games.q: you're on the sidewalk. a bell rings, and the procession comes down the street with the host under its canopy. what do the people around you do?
o: kneel, or take off their caps, as it passes.
turn their backs and carry on shopping.
follow it to the church to get a seat.
games.why: people on the sidewalk kneel; a man on a bike takes off his cap. for Catholics, Christ is present in what's being carried.

practice: Walk your streets in your mind, pausing as a procession does: the busiest place you pass in a week, a station or a supermarket line; then a quiet one, a clinic waiting room; then the place you'll be tonight.
If you pray, pray for the people in each place, as the procession blesses its streets; if you don't, hold each place as if it mattered, because to someone it does.

wordCard.voice: Corpus Christi. Latin for the body of Christ: a feast when Catholics carry the consecrated bread out of the church and through the streets.

orig.note: Greek: body. "This is my body" uses this word.
